analysis.one_liner: Bars private insurers from restricting dialysis coverage relative to other conditions under Medicare coordination rules.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to stop insurers from restricting dialysis benefits never got a Senate committee vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under Medicare's secondary payer rules, when someone with end-stage renal disease has employer health coverage, the private plan and Medicare split responsibility for paying for care. A 2022 Supreme Court decision allowed some employer plans to restrict dialysis benefits in ways that push patients toward cheaper in-center treatment instead of home dialysis. This bill would write the pre-existing patient protections back into law: a group health plan could not limit, restrict, or condition dialysis benefits compared to benefits for other chronic medical conditions. It was introduced in August 2022 by Senator Menendez with Republican Senator Bill Cassidy as cosponsor, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a committee vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Dialysis patients with end-stage renal disease who have employer or group health coverage. The bill would stop their plans from limiting, restricting, or conditioning dialysis benefits compared to benefits for other chronic conditions, which in practice means patients keep a real choice between home dialysis and in-center treatment rather than being steered by benefit design toward the option their plan prefers. Their families and caregivers also benefit from that stability.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for a group health plan to limit, restrict, or condition dialysis benefits relative to benefits for other chronic conditions, restoring the patient-protection intent of the Medicare Secondary Payer rules.

It also closes a loophole by treating patients who need an item or service related to their dialysis eligibility as covered by the same protections, so plans cannot use technical workarounds to deny payment.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor group health plans and the insurers that administer them would pay more dialysis claims directly instead of shifting costs to Medicare or restricting benefits, and those costs would ultimately be spread across everyone who pays premiums and the businesses offering coverage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employer health plans and premium payers

drawbacks.text: Someone pays for the restored coverage: the bill requires employer group health plans to cover dialysis without restriction, and private plans generally pay dialysis providers more than Medicare does, so the added cost flows into employer health costs and premiums paid by other workers and enrollees.

The bill is narrow. It helps only dialysis patients who have employer group coverage; it does nothing for people with end-stage renal disease whose coverage is Medicare or Medicaid, and it addresses only dialysis rather than the broader question of how plans may design benefits for high-cost conditions.

By requiring plans to pay dialysis claims without being able to steer patients to lower-cost settings, the bill also locks in a billing channel that benefits large dialysis companies, which charge private plans higher rates — a cost-benefit tradeoff an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it covers, the bill's benefit is real and targeted: dialysis patients with employer coverage would keep the same freedom to choose home or in-center treatment that patients with other chronic conditions have, under rules that existed before the courts narrowed them. The honest cost is that someone has to pay for that freedom — employer plans and insurers, and ultimately other premium payers, since private plans generally pay dialysis providers more than Medicare does. The bill is also narrow: it does nothing for the many ESRD patients whose coverage is Medicare or Medicaid, and it restores protections only for dialysis rather than addressing the broader cost-shifting issue behind the ruling. A fair reading is a modest, pro-patient bill whose costs are real but diffused, and which died without anyone ever voting on it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2022 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Menendez introduced the bill on August 3, 2022, together with Senator Bill Cassidy.

The bill would amend Medicare's secondary payer rules so that a group health plan violates the law if it limits, restricts, or conditions dialysis benefits compared with benefits for other chronic conditions.
On the day of introduction the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee — the only action it ever received.
No committee vote, floor vote, or further action followed, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employer group health plans and insurers, which after the Supreme Court's 2022 Marietta v. DaVita ruling can continue limiting dialysis benefits and steering patients to cheaper in-center care without congressional correction; large dialysis companies gain nothing from the bill's death, but dialysis patients lose the choice the bill would have protected.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 3, 2022 to restore Medicare Secondary Payer protections for dialysis patients.

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; a physician, he joined the Democratic sponsor at introduction.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a markup or vote on it; the bill received no committee action after its referral on August 3, 2022.

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic senator introduced the bill with two Republican cosponsors including Senator Cassidy, but no floor or committee vote ever occurred, so broader partisan support was never tested.

industries.industry: Dialysis providers (large dialysis organizations such as DaVita and Fresenius)
industries.note: The bill requires private plans to cover dialysis without steering restrictions, which keeps privately insured patients free to choose any dialysis provider and keeps private plans — which generally pay more than Medicare — as the paying party during the coordination period. This protects provider revenue while also directly protecting patient choice of home versus in-center treatment.

industries.industry: Employer group health plans and health insurers
industries.note: Plans would no longer be able to limit or condition dialysis benefits to shift costs to Medicare or steer patients to cheaper in-center care, so they would bear more dialysis spending, which ultimately shows up in employer health costs and premiums.
